blocks.text:
STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL

Heather Miller
Chief Operating Officer
{{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}

Dear Heather,

As we agreed when we last spoke, I am writing to set out the terms on which Quillon Harbor Advisors LLC will act for the board of directors of {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} in connection with the proposed sale of one of the company's operating divisions. I have tried to make the letter as plain about the limits of our work as about its content, because an opinion is only as useful as the board's understanding of what it does and does not say.

The board has asked us for our opinion as to whether the consideration to be received by the company in the sale is fair, from a financial point of view, to the company. To reach it we will review the division's historical results and management's forecast, work with you and the division's finance team to establish what the business would cost to run on its own once it leaves the group, and test the proposed consideration against a discounted cash flow analysis, the trading values of comparable listed companies, and the prices paid in comparable transactions. We will also read each draft of the sale agreement as it is produced, since the opinion must speak to the consideration as the final agreement defines it.

We should say just as clearly what the opinion will not do. It will not be a recommendation to the board on whether to proceed, or to shareholders on how to act, and it will not weigh the sale against other courses the company might take; nor will we negotiate with the buyer or look for other buyers, since either would compromise the independence that gives an opinion its value. We cannot tell you today what our conclusion will be, and nothing in this letter, or in our work along the way, should be read as a promise of one.

Richard Mccoy, a Partner of the firm, will lead the work from day to day and will be your first call on any question of substance. Sandra Norman, an Advisory Associate, will run the information request and keep the record of what has been asked for, what has arrived, and what is still outstanding, while Melissa Jacobson, an Analyst, will build the valuation analyses under Richard's direction. I will remain responsible for the engagement as a whole, I will read the opinion before it goes to our internal opinion committee, and I will attend the board meeting at which it is delivered.

The engagement commences on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}}. The table that follows lists what the board will receive from us, and roughly when; the later stages are paced by the board's own timetable for the sale and by the negotiation with the buyer, and if either moves we will write to you promptly to say how our schedule moves with it.

blocks.text: Our fee, and when it is paid

Our fee for this engagement is {{fact:f:E-2021-001.fee}}, payable in two parts: the first on signature of this letter and the balance on delivery of the opinion. The fee is fixed and falls due whatever the opinion concludes and whether or not the sale proceeds, so that nothing we are paid depends on the answer we give. We will also bill reasonable out-of-pocket expenses at cost, monthly, and will ask you before incurring any beyond travel and document costs.
How long this letter runs

This letter takes effect when you countersign it and runs until we have delivered the opinion and any bring-down the board asks for, or until the sale is abandoned, whichever comes first. Either of us may end it earlier by written notice; if the board does so, the first part of the fee and any expenses already incurred remain payable, and we may withdraw if we cannot obtain the information an opinion requires.
Use of the opinion

The opinion will be addressed to the board and given solely for its use in considering the sale. It may not be quoted, summarized, or disclosed to anyone else without our prior written consent, except where the law requires it, and in that case we ask to review the description of the opinion before it is published.
Confidentiality

We will hold everything the company gives us in confidence and use it only for this engagement. Wherever our working papers might circulate beyond the team named above, they will describe the division by sector and size rather than by name, and we will not discuss the sale with the buyer or its advisers except as the board directs.
Reliance and the limit of our liability

We will rely on the information the company and its advisers provide without verifying it independently, and we will not appraise individual assets or give legal, tax, or accounting advice. Our liability to the company in connection with this engagement is limited to the fees we have received under this letter, except for losses finally found by a court to have resulted from our gross negligence or willful misconduct, and the company will indemnify us against claims by third parties arising from the engagement on the same terms.
Independence

We will accept no engagement from the buyer while this one continues. Before we deliver the opinion, we will confirm to the board in writing any relationship with the buyer that the board should weigh in reading it.
Governing law
This letter is governed by the laws of the state in which our principal office is located, and the courts of that state will hear any dispute between us that we cannot settle by discussion.

Once the board is content with these terms, I would ask you to countersign this letter on its behalf and return a copy to me. The day it reaches us, Sandra Norman will send you our information request, and Richard Mccoy will call you to fix the first session with the division's finance team.
Agreed on behalf of the board of directors of {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}, by its authorized officer:
{{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} fairness opinion: opening note
From Sandra Norman to Richard Mccoy and Melissa Jacobson. For the deal team only; please do not forward.

This opinion will be decided by the cost base, not by the multiples. The division we are valuing has never run on its own: its results carry a share of the group's central costs on an allocation key, and a buyer will price it on what those services will actually cost once the division leaves the group, which may be a quite different figure. If we value the division on its reported results and the stand-alone cost turns out higher, the board will hold an opinion that compares the consideration with a business the buyer is not buying.

So we will start where we would normally finish. Before Melissa Jacobson opens a comparables screen, she will build a bridge from the division's reported results to a stand-alone view, line by line, covering finance, IT, procurement, insurance and whatever else the group provides today, and each line will show whether its figure came from management or from our own estimate. Richard Mccoy will take the first management session himself and give most of it to those services and to what the buyer has said it will and will not cover through transitional arrangements, and I have ordered the information request so that the cost material comes first and the historical detail follows.

It also changes how we treat the buyer's view of those costs. The buyer will have formed its own estimate of what it takes to run the division alone; we will not ask for it, and if it reaches us through the company we will not adopt it, because an opinion resting on the buyer's arithmetic would not be independent. Where management's figure and ours differ on a line, the bridge will carry both and the board will see the difference, so that no choice between them is made quietly inside the model.

The objectives follow from that order. The engagement opened on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}}, and the first thing the board will receive from us is a note on the basis of valuation, setting out the forecast and the stand-alone cost base we propose to rely on, which the board confirms before any valuation work is put in front of it. After that comes a preliminary review with the board in which the method is shown before the answer, and then an opinion our committee can pass without reopening the cost question, because by that point the board will already have settled it. The committee will want every cost line traced to a source, so the bridge will be built to that standard from its first draft and not tidied at the end.

What we need from {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} at the start is access more than documents. Heather Miller is our day-to-day contact, and I have asked her for an introduction to whoever in the division prepares the monthly management accounts, since that is the person who can tell us how each allocation was set. The information request went to her when the signed letter came back, and nothing has returned yet, which is normal at this stage; beyond it we need the term sheet, each draft of the sale agreement as counsel produces it, and the board's timetable for the sale in writing, so that our schedule rests on dates the board has set rather than on our own guesses.

Heather Miller is carrying this alongside her own job, so every request to her will come in one consolidated list with the reason for each item beside it, never in separate emails. I will circulate that log, showing what has been asked for, what has arrived and what is outstanding, every Friday, beginning this week.
{{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}: on what cost base should the division be valued?

Prepared for Heather Miller, Chief Operating Officer, by Richard Mccoy, Sandra Norman and Melissa Jacobson. Since the engagement began on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}}, we have held the management sessions and received most of what the information request asked for. The term sheet already sets out the consideration the buyer proposes, so the open question is not what the buyer will pay but what the board should compare it with. The valuation analyses cannot go further until the board fixes the cost base they rest on, and the preliminary review with the board, the next stage in our schedule, depends on that decision.
Our answer: value the division as a stand-alone business, with group services at their full replacement cost

items: The reported results carry group services on an allocation key, not at what the division would pay for them on its own.
The bridge built with the division's finance team prices each service line by line and marks which figures are management's and which are our estimates.
The buyer's term sheet covers only part of that cost base with transitional services, and only for a limited period.
The comparable companies and precedent transactions are stand-alone businesses, so the comparison is like for like only on this basis.
A downside case, with replacement costs above management's estimates, will show the board how far the analysis moves.

blocks.text: What we need to proceed

We ask Heather Miller to put our note on the basis of valuation to the board at its next meeting and to send us the board's confirmation in writing, since the opinion will refer to it. We also need management to sign off the replacement cost estimates in the bridge, and the first draft of the sale agreement as soon as counsel has it. If the board prefers a different basis, we need to know before the preliminary review, because every analysis we will show it is built on this one. Once the basis is confirmed, Melissa Jacobson will complete the analyses on it, Richard Mccoy will propose a date for the preliminary review, and Sandra Norman will confirm the remaining information items to Heather Miller in writing.
Working session: {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} fairness opinion
Present

blocks.text: Discussion

The session reviewed the preliminary valuation work and the items still open before the board's preliminary review. Richard Mccoy chaired and kept these notes. They record what was decided, and the reasons where they matter.

Heather Miller reported that the board has confirmed the stand-alone basis of valuation. The confirmation is minuted. She will send the extract, because the opinion will refer to it. Management has also signed off the replacement cost estimates in the bridge, with one change: the insurance line now uses the broker's quotation in place of our estimate.

Melissa Jacobson presented the preliminary analyses. The discounted cash flow runs on the board plan, restated to the stand-alone basis. The comparable companies are listed businesses of similar activity and size, identified in the working papers by sector only. The precedent set is thin. Few deals of this size were divisional sales, and prices paid for whole companies are not a clean guide to the price of a carve-out. Richard Mccoy proposed that the discounted cash flow carry the most weight and that the market analyses serve as a check on it. Heather Miller asked whether the board would see all three. It will, each with its range, and the weighting will be explained on the page.

Melissa Jacobson has also run the downside case, which sets the replacement costs above management's estimates. The group agreed to show it beside the base case at the preliminary review, with no conclusion attached to either.

Sandra Norman reported on the information request. Everything asked for has arrived except the draft sale agreement and the transitional services schedule. Both are with the buyer's counsel. Heather Miller expects a first draft within two weeks. Until then the only statement of the consideration is the term sheet, which provides for an adjustment to the price at closing for working capital. The opinion must address the consideration as the final agreement defines it. The mechanics of that adjustment therefore have to be read before the committee review.

Richard Mccoy raised the timetable. The preliminary review with the board can proceed on the term sheet. The committee review cannot. Heather Miller will ask the company's counsel to press the buyer's counsel for the draft.

blocks.text: The preliminary review is the next fixed point. Richard Mccoy will propose a date for it to Heather Miller once the materials are in draft.
{{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} fairness opinion: status report at the midpoint

The draft sale agreement has not arrived, and it is now the one item holding the opinion back. At our working session earlier this month you expected the buyer's counsel to circulate a first draft within two weeks; that time has passed, and without the draft we cannot confirm how the agreement will define the consideration, how the working capital adjustment at closing will be calculated, or what the transitional services schedule will oblige the buyer to provide. So far the delay has cost the board nothing it cannot recover, since the analyses are ready and the preliminary review does not need the draft; it begins to cost time once that review is behind us, because nothing after it can move without the agreement.

Richard Mccoy spoke to the company's counsel last week, and counsel has since raised the timing with the buyer's counsel directly; we understand the delay lies in the buyer's own review of the transitional services terms rather than in any point of disagreement, though we have that only at second hand. Melissa Jacobson has set up the analyses so that any change the draft makes to the consideration or to the transitional services can be run through the base and downside cases within a day or two of its arrival. I have also tied the opinion committee review in our schedule to receipt of the draft rather than to a calendar date, so the committee will sit as soon as the drafting allows and the delay will not grow once the draft is in hand.

Everything else is where the schedule put it. The extract of the board's confirmation of the stand-alone basis is on file, management has signed off the replacement cost estimates, and the preliminary analyses are drafted on the updated bridge, with the insurance line now on the broker's quotation. Melissa Jacobson's downside case is run and sits beside the base case in the draft materials, and the comparable company and precedent transaction sets are fixed, so the preliminary review needs nothing further from us except a date.

blocks.text: For the board to decide before our next report

The board needs to decide whether the preliminary review goes ahead at its next meeting on the strength of the term sheet, or waits for the draft agreement. We recommend going ahead, because the method and the ranges do not depend on the drafting, the board will see the downside case well before it has to weigh the opinion, and any change the draft makes to the consideration can come back to the board as a short update rather than as a second review. If the board would rather wait, it should do so knowing that the committee review, and with it the delivery of the opinion, will move by however long the draft is late.

The board should also tell us whether it wants the downside case in the opinion presentation itself or only at the preliminary review; we see merit in either and will follow the board's preference. Once we have its answer, Richard Mccoy will fix the date of the preliminary review with you, and my next report will follow it.
For Heather Miller, Chief Operating Officer. From Sandra Norman, Advisory Associate, with Richard Mccoy and Melissa Jacobson.
